title: The Sentinel of the Secret Chambers: The Biographical, Mystical, and Geopolitical Legacy of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz
source_file: The Sentinel of the Secret Chambers_ The Biographical, Mystical, and Geopolitical Legacy of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz.docx
content:
Biographical Foundations and the North African Rabbinic Milieu
The life of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz represents a rare synthesis of traditional North African rabbinic authority, modern secular education, active military service, and esoteric Jerusalem Kabbalah.[1] Born on August 15, 1924 (ט"ו באב ה'תרפ"ד), in the Tunisian town of Menzel Bouzelfa, Getz was raised in an environment saturated with classical scholarship.[2] He was the third of four brothers born to Rabbi Tzemach Getz, who descended from a distinguished rabbinic lineage, and Simha-Messauda, a direct descendant of the revered eighteenth-century commentator Rabbi Chaim ibn Attar, the Ohr HaChaim.[2] Shortly after his birth, the family relocated to Tunis, where he commenced his formal education at the "Or HaTorah" Talmud Torah.[1, 2] Displaying an early inclination toward intellectual synthesis, Getz successfully demanded that the institution incorporate French language instruction alongside sacred studies, a request that signaled his lifelong capacity to navigate both sacred and mundane spheres.[2] He advanced his religious studies under the tutelage of Rabbi Yehoshua Pitoussi, who would later serve as the Chief Rabbi of Safed.[1]
The historical convulsions of World War II profoundly shaped his personal trajectory. During the Axis occupation of Tunisia, Getz was conscripted by Nazi forces into a grueling forced labor battalion in the port city of Bizerte.[1] On the festival of Tu B'Shvat in 1943 (ה'תש"ג), exploiting the chaos of an Allied air raid, he escaped captivity by disguising himself in a military uniform he had acquired, fleeing on foot to his family home.[1] This narrow escape prompted a lifelong vow to celebrate Tu B'Shvat annually as a personal day of deliverance.[1]
Following the war, at the age of nineteen, Getz married his distant relative, Esther-Silvette Guez, and settled in Nabeul, where he balanced commercial work as a shop clerk with advanced academic pursuits, studying law via correspondence with the Sorbonne University in Paris.[1] In 1946 (ה'תש"ו), at the age of twenty-two, he received formal rabbinic ordination and was appointed communal rabbi of Souk El-Arba'a.[1] In this post, he served as a multi-faceted spiritual leader, functioning simultaneously as rabbi, cantor, ritual circumciser (mohel), slaughterer (shochet), and marriage registrar.[1] Concurrently, he emerged as a prominent Zionist organizer, encouraging Hebrew education, advocating for emigration to Israel, and encouraging local Jewish youth to train in self-defense and firearms.[1] His organizational acumen caught the attention of the Jewish Agency, leading to an assignment in France, where he managed an educational facility for the Youth Aliyah movement.[1]
Pioneers of the Galilee: Secular Integration and the Catalyst of Loss
Upon his immigration to Israel in 1949 (ה'תש"ט), Getz initially resided in Haifa before accepting a comprehensive rabbinic appointment in the northern agricultural cooperative of Kerem Ben Zimra.[1] In the Galilee, he modeled a pioneer lifestyle, serving as the local rabbi, cantor, mohel, and shochet, while also founding and directing the "Benayahu" agricultural elementary school.[1] His integration into the state apparatus deepened in 1952 when he enlisted in the Israel Defense Forces, completed an officers' course, and was appointed as the security coordinator for the Marom HaGalil regional council.[1]
The turning point of his life occurred during the Six-Day War of 1967. His second son, Avner, a paratrooper in the reserve forces, was killed in action during the intense hand-to-hand combat to liberate the Old City of Jerusalem.[1] Despite his profound grief, Getz famously remarked: "Woe to me that this happened to me, and blessed am I that I merited my son falling for the liberation of Jerusalem".[1] Driven by a desire to reside near his son's final resting place on Mount Herzl, Getz and his wife relocated to Jerusalem.[1] His administrative capability and spiritual stature attracted national recognition, and in 1969 (תשכ"ט), Minister of Religions Zerach Warhaftig appointed him as the official Rabbi of the Western Wall, a jurisdiction that was later expanded to encompass all Holy Sites in Israel.[1] Decades later, Getz would also endure the loss of another son, Yair, who was tragically killed in a truck accident, and was subsequently laid to rest alongside him on the Mount of Olives.[1]
The Restoration of Yeshivat Beit El and Kabbalistic Devotion
In Jerusalem, Getz submerged himself in the study of Jewish mysticism, aligning himself with the great kabbalists of the city, most notably Rabbi Ovadia Hadaya.[1] Rabbi Hadaya had been forced to relocate the historic Yeshivat HaMekubalim "Beit El" from the Old City to the New City following the Jordanian occupation of the Jewish Quarter in 1948.[1] Following the reunification of the city, Getz worked to reclaim and reconstruct the original three-hundred-year-old sanctuary of the yeshiva in the Jewish Quarter—initially established by Rabbi Gedaliah Hayon and famously led by the master kabbalist Rabbi Shalom Sharabi (the Rashash).[1] Recognizing his expertise in both the open (nigleh) and concealed (nistar) dimensions of the Torah, the rabbinic leadership appointed Getz as the Rosh Yeshiva of Beit El.[1]
His personal conduct was defined by ascetic rigor. He adopted a highly structured routine, retiring for sleep only between the evening prayer (Maariv) and midnight.[1] At midnight, he descended into the subterranean chambers of the Western Wall to recite Tikkun Chatzot (the Midnight Liturgy) directly opposite the estimated location of the Holy of Holies, studying kabbalistic texts there until the sunrise prayer (Vatikin).[1] After completing his administrative duties as Rabbi of the Western Wall, he dedicated his afternoons to teaching at Yeshivat Beit El.[1]
Despite his personal asceticism, Getz advocated a philosophy of domestic harmony and peace. He maintained strict entrance requirements for Yeshivat Beit El, making a student's admission contingent upon the maintenance of peace within their home (Shalom Bayit).[1] In his private life, he modeled this behavior by showing profound respect for his wife, establishing a custom of presenting her with a gift or piece of jewelry at the start of every Hebrew month (Rosh Chodesh).[1]
Getz left behind a significant corpus of written works spanning kabbalistic theory, biblical commentary, and historical documentation.[1, 2] His primary kabbalistic work, Reshpey Esh ("Flashes of Fire"), is a commentary on the esoteric intentions (kavanot) of the Rashash, structured around the classical systems of Rabbi Isaac Luria (the Ari) and Rabbi Chaim Vital.[1] Written in dense, classical rabbinic style, Reshpey Esh remains a core text for advanced students at Yeshivat Beit El, studied under the guidance of his student, Rabbi Yisrael Avichai.[1] His other works include Gitzei Torah ("Sparks of the Torah"), a volume of homiletical and mystical commentaries on the Pentateuch, and Kuntres HaKotel ("The Western Wall Treatise"), which outlines the halakhic history of the site.[2] He also composed specialized essays on domestic harmony (Ma'amar Shalom Bayit), the sanctity of the Land of Israel (Ma'amar Eretz Yisrael), and the spiritual significance of Jerusalem (Ma'amar Yerushalayim), alongside two liturgical poems written during and after the Six-Day War.[2]
The Archeology of Redemption: The Gate of the Priests and the Warren's Gate Crisis
The most historically complex chapter of Getz’s tenure began in the early 1970s with the systematic excavation of the Western Wall Tunnels, a project he initiated and directed.[3] In 1971 (תשל"א), workers uncovered a massive sealed gate along the Western Wall.[3] Getz identified this structure as the "Gate of the Priests," believing it to be the ancient portal through which ritually impure priests departed the Temple Mount complex.[3] His historical calculations suggested that this gateway lay on a direct trajectory to the subterranean chambers where King Josiah had hidden the Ark of the Covenant before the destruction of the First Temple.[3] According to the Mishnah, the Ark had been safely hidden "in winding underground chambers" (במטמוניות עקלקלות).[3] Eager to pursue this discovery, he drafted a letter to the Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, in New York.[3] The Rebbe responded with a firm warning, stating that the sanctity of the Temple Mount must be strictly guarded and that any subterranean excavations beneath the holy site should be suspended.[3] Getz accepted this ruling and paused the project.[3]
However, the situation changed dramatically in August 1981 (תשמ"א). During ongoing preservation and clearance works, excavators accidentally breached a wall adjacent to "Warren’s Gate"—a subterranean portal named after the nineteenth-century British archaeologist Charles Warren.[3, 4] This gateway was a key entrance to the Temple Mount during the late Second Temple period, famously documented by Josephus.[5] Behind the breached wall lay a massive cavern, measuring approximately 28.5×5.5 meters with a height of 10.70 meters, which had functioned as a water cistern (designated as Cistern 30 in Warren's survey).[5] In ancient times, this chamber served as a subterranean passage from which people climbed to the Mount via stairs.[5]
Getz believed this cavern was a key to the Temple's ancient foundations and a direct pathway to the hidden Ark.[3] He immediately organized operations to pump out the water and mud that filled the chamber.[3] Because of the sensitive nature of the site, the work was kept quiet, but news of the excavation gradually leaked to political figures and eventually appeared in the national media.[3]
The public revelation of the excavation triggered an immediate geopolitical crisis, drawing protests from Islamic authorities (the Waqf) and sparking concerns of widespread civil unrest.[3] Tensions escalated when Waqf workers breached the cistern from an entrance on top of the Temple Mount.[3] Getz rushed to the site, where he found himself facing an angry crowd.[3] Armed with his personal sidearm, he held his ground until yeshiva students and security forces arrived to secure the area.[3] To prevent further escalation, the Israeli government intervened.[3] Workers from the Waqf built a concrete wall approximately 3 to 4 meters thick across the middle of the cavern.[3] Concurrently, Israeli authorities ordered the entrance sealed from the Western Wall side, permanently closing the passage and ending Getz's efforts to locate the Ark.[3, 4]
The Halakhic Debate and the Structural Sanctity of the Getz Synagogue
The closure of Warren's Gate did not end spiritual activity at the site. Instead, it led to a significant halakhic discussion regarding the boundaries of the Temple Mount and the status of subterranean spaces.[5] The central question was whether entering the gateway of Warren's Gate violated the strict prohibition against ritually impure individuals (teme'im) entering the Temple Mount complex.[5]
To address this issue, Getz hosted a detailed meeting inside the tunnels with the Sephardic Chief Rabbi (Rishon LeZion), Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, and the prominent halakhic authority, Rabbi Eliezer Waldenberg.[5] According to Getz's personal diaries, the three scholars spent two hours analyzing the structural layout and halakhic status of the gateway and the chambers beyond.[5] This historic meeting is discussed in Rabbi Shmuel Rabinowitz's "Shu"t Sha'arei Zion" (Volume 3, Chapter 6).[5]
The rabbinic consensus turned on the concept of "under the archway" (תחת האגוף).[5] Rabbi Ovadia Yosef ruled that the gateway arch itself did not share the full sanctity of the Temple Mount's inner courts.[5] Consequently, they permitted:
Unlimited entry into the vestibule of the gate without requiring ritual immersion (tevilah).[5]
The continuation of excavation and reinforcement work within the gateway structure.[5]
The establishment of a permanent synagogue directly adjacent to the sealed entrance.[5]
Following this ruling, Getz established a small, narrow synagogue directly in front of the sealed Warren’s Gate.[4, 5] Located beneath the Muslim Quarter of the Old City, this sanctuary sits exactly 97 meters from the estimated historical site of the Holy of Holies, making it the closest prayer space to Judaism's most sacred point.[6] The physical layout of the synagogue consists of vaults leaning on the Western Wall, creating a shape resembling the Hebrew letter Dalet (ℸ).[6] The system of eastern vaults next to the Wall forms an elongated gallery of approximately 15×2 meters.[6] The southern vault reaches a height of 6.84 meters and contains a sealed water opening at the top, while the northern vault stands at 3.45 meters.[6] This elongated space opens into a square main hall measuring 4.0×4.0 meters.[6]

The synagogue operates under strict administrative guidelines managed by the Western Wall Heritage Foundation.[6, 7] Access to this subterranean sanctuary is highly regulated to preserve its sacred character and comply with physical safety protocols.[7]
Synthesis and Final Legacy
Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz passed away on September 18, 1995 (כ"ג באלול ה'תשנ"ה), following a sudden heart attack.[1] His passing occurred shortly after he completed the reconstruction of the Yeshivat Beit El building in the Jewish Quarter.[1] He was laid to rest on the Mount of Olives.[1]
His written legacy includes his personal diary, the twelve-volume Western Wall Diary (Yoman HaKotel HaMa'aravi).[2] This diary documents twenty-eight years of administrative and spiritual work, detailing excavations, meetings with world leaders, and his search for the Ark of the Covenant.[2] This work was later compiled by author Simcha Raz into the 502-page biography Rav HaKotel.[8] Through his structural discoveries, halakhic decisions, and mystical scholarship, Getz remains a central figure in the modern history of the Western Wall.[1]
